lead: A wing torsion box is often split by a middle spar into two closed cells, and a fuselage is split by a floor beam the same way. Torque is shared between the cells, and because the cells are joined along a common wall they must twist at the same rate. One torque equation plus one equal-twist equation fix the two circulating flows q₁ and q₂, and from them the shear flow in every wall of the section.
prereq: You need: 5.4 for the single-cell torsion formula, and 5.3 for the cut-and-add-q₀ method used with a shear load.

sections.h3: Two cells share one wall and one twist rate

blocks.text: A single closed tube has one unknown shear flow q, fixed by one equation, T = 2Aq. A box with two cells has two unknowns. Call q₁ the flow circulating round cell 1 and q₂ the flow round cell 2, both in N/mm and both drawn in the same sense, say clockwise.

On the outer walls, cell 1 carries q₁ and cell 2 carries q₂. On the wall they share, the two circulations run in opposite directions along the same wall, so the net shear flow there is q₁ − q₂. A wing box with a middle spar and a fuselage with a floor beam both have exactly this layout.

blocks.where: T is the applied torque in N·mm; A₁ and A₂ are the areas enclosed by cells 1 and 2 in mm²; q₁ and q₂ are the circulating shear flows in N/mm.

θ′ᵢ is the rate of twist of cell i in rad/mm; G is the shear modulus in N/mm²; t is wall thickness in mm; ds is an element of wall length in mm; the subscript i on the integral means the path goes round cell i only, using the net flow in any shared wall.

blocks.text: The cells are joined along the shared wall, so they cannot twist by different amounts: θ′₁ = θ′₂. That is the second equation. It is the one most answers leave out.

sections.h3: Setting up and solving the system

blocks.text: Write each cell's integral in terms of the flows. For cell i, ∮ᵢ(q/t)ds = Sᵢqᵢ − Σⱼ (Lᵢⱼ / tᵢⱼ) qⱼ, where Sᵢ = ∮ᵢ ds/t over the walls of cell i, a dimensionless number when ds and t are both in mm (500 for cell 1 and 400 for cell 2 in the example), Lᵢⱼ is the length of the wall shared by cells i and j, and tᵢⱼ is that wall's thickness. The minus sign is the difference rule again.

items: Number the cells 1 to n and draw every flow q₁, q₂, … in one sense.
Compute Sᵢ = ∮ ds/t for each cell over its own walls.
Set θ′ᵢ = θ′ⱼ for each pair of neighbouring cells: n − 1 equations.
Add the torque equation T = Σ 2Aᵢqᵢ: n equations for n unknowns.
Solve, then report outer walls as qᵢ and a shared wall as qᵢ − qⱼ.

blocks.text: The system is linear, so a matrix solver does all the work: put the coefficients of q₁ … qₙ in a matrix K and the right-hand side in a vector r, then solve Kq = r. In MATLAB this is one backslash solve; on paper it is elimination. Some syllabi mark this step as a small programming exercise. The method does not change, only the solver does. A three-cell box adds one more flow and a second equal-twist condition.

sections.h3: Shear loads, shear centre and real sections

blocks.text: The same equations work when the section carries a transverse shear load instead of pure torque. Cut each cell to make the section open, get the basic flow q_b from 5.3, then add one constant per cell: q = q_b + q₀ᵢ. Equal twist relates q₀₁ and q₀₂, and a second condition — zero twist rate, or a known applied torque — closes the system.

Shear centre. Take the applied shear V through an arbitrary reference point, cut the cells and add q₀ᵢ, then choose the q₀ᵢ so that every cell has zero twist rate. Take moments of the resulting shear flows about the reference point; call the moment M. The load line of the shear flows, and hence the shear centre, lies at distance e = M/V from the reference point, on the side that makes the moments balance. Repeat for a second load direction if the shear centre position is needed in two coordinates.

Walls that take no direct stress. A plain web with no booms attached carries no bending stress, but it still carries shear, so its length and thickness still enter ∮ds/t. In the idealized section the booms carry only direct (bending) stress and are left out of the shear-carrying path; every skin, web and spar wall carries shear, so all of their lengths and thicknesses stay in ∮ds/t (see 5.6).

Where it appears. A wing box between front and rear spars, divided by a middle spar, is this problem exactly: the spars take the bending, the two cells share the torque from the aileron. A fuselage divided by a floor or cargo floor behaves the same way, with roof and floor twisting together under torsion.

figure.caption: Torque of 20 kN·m is shared between the two cells as q₁ and q₂; the equal-twist condition gives the second equation, and the shared wall then carries the difference q₁ − q₂.

spec.aria: Block diagram: a torque of 20 kN·m is split between two cells as q₁ and q₂, the equal-twist condition θ₁ = θ₂ gives a second equation, solving gives q₁ = 160.5 N/mm and q₂ = 143.2 N/mm, and the shared wall carries their difference, 17.4 N/mm.

examples.question: A two-cell box section has cell 1 of width 200 mm and cell 2 of width 125 mm, both 200 mm high, separated by a vertical shared wall 200 mm long. The outer walls are 1.5 mm thick, the shared wall is 2 mm, and G is constant. The applied torque is 20 kN·m. Find q₁, q₂, the shear flow and shear stress in the shared wall, and the rate of twist.
steps: Areas: A₁ = 200 × 200 = 40 000 mm², A₂ = 125 × 200 = 25 000 mm². Torque T = 20 kN·m = 20 × 10⁶ N·mm.
Cell 1 walls: outer 200 + 200 + 200 = 600 mm at 1.5 mm gives 600/1.5 = 400; shared wall 200 mm at 2 mm gives 100. So S₁ = 500.
Cell 2 walls: outer 125 + 125 + 200 = 450 mm at 1.5 mm gives 300; shared wall gives 100. So S₂ = 400.
Twist rates: θ′₁ = (500q₁ − 100q₂)/(2 × 40 000 G) and θ′₂ = (400q₂ − 100q₁)/(2 × 25 000 G). The minus terms come from the shared wall carrying q₁ − q₂.
Set θ′₁ = θ′₂: 50 000(500q₁ − 100q₂) = 80 000(400q₂ − 100q₁), so 25q₁ − 5q₂ = 32q₂ − 8q₁, giving 33q₁ = 37q₂, that is q₂ = 0.8919q₁.
Substitute q₂: 80 000q₁ + 50 000(0.8919q₁) = 124 595q₁ = 20 × 10⁶, so q₁ = 160.5 N/mm and q₂ = 143.2 N/mm.
Shared wall: q = q₁ − q₂ = 17.4 N/mm, giving shear stress 17.4/2 = 8.7 N/mm².
Twist check: θ′ = (500 × 160.5 − 100 × 143.2)/(2 × 40 000 G) = 65 943/(80 000G) = 0.824/G rad/mm; cell 2 gives the same value.
examples.answer: q₁ = 160.5 N/mm, q₂ = 143.2 N/mm, the shared wall carries 17.4 N/mm (8.7 N/mm²), and both cells twist at 0.824/G rad/mm.

traps: Adding q₁ and q₂ in the shared wall. The two circulations oppose each other along that wall, so it carries q₁ − q₂.
Using the torque equation alone. A two-cell box needs two equations and a three-cell box needs three; the equal-twist condition is not optional.
Taking ∮ds/t over the whole outer perimeter for one cell. The integral goes round that cell only, and a shared wall is counted once in each cell at its own thickness.
Mixing units: A in mm² with T in kN·m. Convert first, so 20 kN·m becomes 20 × 10⁶ N·mm.
Reversing the assumed sense of q₂ only. Pick one sense for every cell and keep that sign through the whole solution.

quiz.q: What shear flow does the wall shared by two cells carry?
quiz.a: The difference q₁ − q₂ of the two cell circulations, because the circulations run in opposite directions along that wall.

quiz.q: Why must both cells have the same rate of twist?
quiz.a: They are joined along the shared wall, which cannot shear apart or change length. If one cell twisted faster, the shared wall would have to distort, so both cells rotate by the same angle per unit length.

quiz.q: A two-cell box has A₁ = 50 000 mm² and A₂ = 30 000 mm². Equal twist gives q₂ = 0.8q₁. The torque is 14.8 kN·m. Find q₁ and q₂.
quiz.a: T = 2A₁q₁ + 2A₂q₂ = 100 000q₁ + 60 000(0.8q₁) = 148 000q₁ = 14.8 × 10⁶ N·mm, so q₁ = 100 N/mm and q₂ = 80 N/mm.

quiz.q: A three-cell box carries a torque. How many unknowns and how many equations are there, and what are the equations?
quiz.a: Three flows q₁, q₂, q₃ and three equations: one torque equation T = Σ2Aᵢqᵢ plus two equal-twist conditions, for example θ′₁ = θ′₂ and θ′₂ = θ′₃. Shared walls enter as differences.

quiz.q: A thin web carries no direct stress because no booms are attached to it. Does it still appear in ∮ds/t?
quiz.a: Yes. It carries shear, and the twist rate depends on the shear in every wall of the cell. Only its bending stress is zero; its length and thickness still enter the integral.

quiz.q: How would you locate the shear centre of a two-cell section?
quiz.a: The shear centre is the point through which a transverse load must pass so that the section does not twist; it is found at distance e = M/V from the reference point, where M is the moment of the zero-twist shear flows about that point.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production wing boxes are multi-cell with many stringers, and the same linear system is assembled as a stiffness matrix with hundreds of unknowns in finite element codes. Aircraft rules also require a fail-safe check: one cell may be assumed cracked, and the remaining cells must carry the torque alone. Search next for multi-cell torque box shear flow, Bredt-Batho for multi-cell sections, and shear centre of a multi-cell wing section.
